stem: Which two stop_reason values are the relevant signals for controlling an agentic loop?

options.label: A
options.body: "tool_use" (continue the loop) and "end_turn" (exit the loop).
options.rationale: Correct. stop_reason is the authoritative, deterministic loop signal: "tool_use" means Claude wants to call tools; "end_turn" means it's finished.

options.label: B
options.body: "continue" and "stop" (generic loop-control keywords).
options.rationale: Those aren't stop_reason values in the Messages API.

options.label: C
options.body: "running" and "complete" (job-lifecycle status values).
options.rationale: Not real stop_reason values — the loop is driven by tool_use / end_turn.

options.label: D
options.body: "text" and "tool_use" (two content-block type names).
options.rationale: "text" is a content block type, not a stop_reason. Text can appear alongside tool_use, so it can't signal completion.

stem: An agent loop terminates early: the developer stops it whenever `response.content[0].type == "text"`, assuming a text block means Claude is done. Sometimes Claude still had tools to call. What's the correct termination check?

options.label: A
options.body: Check stop_reason — continue while it's "tool_use", exit on "end_turn".
options.rationale: Correct. Claude can return text alongside tool_use blocks in the same response, so text presence doesn't indicate completion. stop_reason is the deterministic signal built for this.

options.label: B
options.body: Check whether the last content block (not the first) is text.
options.rationale: Block ordering isn't a completion signal — a response can mix text and tool_use in any order. Use stop_reason.

options.label: C
options.body: Parse the assistant text for phrases like "I'm done" or "task complete".
options.rationale: Natural-language parsing is ambiguous and unreliable — exactly what stop_reason exists to replace.

options.label: D
options.body: Set tool_choice to "any" so Claude never returns text.
options.rationale: Forcing a tool every turn creates an infinite loop — Claude can never signal it's finished.

stem: A multi-agent system produces a report on "the impact of AI on creative industries" that only covers visual arts — music, writing, and film are missing. Each subagent did thorough work on its assigned topic. Where is the root cause?

options.label: A
options.body: The coordinator decomposed the topic too narrowly, so entire categories were never assigned to any subagent.
options.rationale: Correct. Each subagent did its job well — the failure is upstream in the coordinator's decomposition. The exam expects you to trace failures to their origin, and the fix is better decomposition, not more subagents.

options.label: B
options.body: The visual-arts subagent overran its assigned scope and crowded out the music, writing, and film subagents from the report.
options.rationale: Subagents are isolated and don't crowd each other out; the missing topics were simply never delegated.

options.label: C
options.body: Add more subagents specifically to cover the missing music, writing, and film categories that never made it into the report.
options.rationale: This treats the symptom. The root cause is the decomposition; fix that and the coordinator assigns the missing categories itself.

options.label: D
options.body: The subagents failed to communicate their individual coverage gaps to one another over the course of the research run.
options.rationale: In hub-and-spoke, subagents never communicate directly — coverage is the coordinator's responsibility.

stem: A coordinator is configured but physically cannot spawn any subagents. Its AgentDefinitions look fine. What's the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.body: The coordinator's allowedTools does not include "Task".
options.rationale: Correct. The Task tool is the mechanism for spawning subagents; "Task" must be in allowedTools. It's a hard requirement — without it, the coordinator can't spawn at all.

options.label: B
options.body: The subagents are missing a description field.
options.rationale: A missing description would hurt selection quality, not make spawning physically impossible.

options.label: C
options.body: The coordinator and subagents are on different model versions.
options.rationale: Model version doesn't gate the ability to spawn — the Task tool permission does.

options.label: D
options.body: The coordinator's fork_session capability wasn't enabled for the run.
options.rationale: fork_session branches a session for divergent exploration; it isn't what enables subagent spawning.

stem: A support agent processes refunds without identity verification in 8% of cases, despite a clear system-prompt instruction to always verify first. What's the correct fix?

options.label: A
options.body: Add a programmatic prerequisite gate that blocks process_refund until verification has completed.
options.rationale: Correct. Verification is a security/financial rule that must hold 100% of the time — that requires deterministic, code-level enforcement (a hook/gate the model can't bypass), not probabilistic prompt guidance.

options.label: B
options.body: Rewrite the system prompt to be far more emphatic and explicit about always verifying the customer's identity before any refund.
options.rationale: Prompt-based guidance is probabilistic — it has a non-zero failure rate, which is exactly the 8%.

options.label: C
options.body: Add few-shot examples to the prompt that demonstrate verifying the customer's identity before the agent processes a refund.
options.rationale: Few-shot examples still rely on the model complying every time; they can't guarantee 100% enforcement.

options.label: D
options.body: Add a routing classifier that flags incoming refund requests for extra scrutiny before the agent is allowed to process them.
options.rationale: A classifier adds another probabilistic component; it doesn't deterministically block an unverified refund.

stem: An agent occasionally processes international transfers without the required AML check. Compliance mandates 100% enforcement. PostToolUse hook, PreToolUse hook, or enhanced prompt?

options.label: A
options.body: A PreToolUse hook that blocks the transfer until the AML check passes.
options.rationale: Correct. PreToolUse runs before the tool executes, so it can block a non-compliant action. Compliance rules that must hold 100% of the time need deterministic pre-execution enforcement.

options.label: B
options.body: A PostToolUse hook that verifies AML after the transfer.
options.rationale: PostToolUse runs after execution — too late to prevent a non-compliant transfer that already happened.

options.label: C
options.body: An enhanced prompt instructing the agent to always run AML checks first.
options.rationale: Prompts are probabilistic guidance; they can't guarantee 100% compliance.

options.label: D
options.body: A PostToolUse hook that normalizes the transfer response format.
options.rationale: Normalization is the right use of PostToolUse, but it does nothing to enforce the AML prerequisite.

stem: Different MCP tools return timestamps in Unix epoch, ISO 8601, and DD/MM/YYYY, and statuses as both numeric codes and strings. The model keeps misreading them. What's the cleanest fix?

options.label: A
options.body: A PostToolUse hook that normalizes all tool outputs to consistent formats before the model processes them.
options.rationale: Correct. PostToolUse runs after a tool executes but before the model sees the result — ideal for converting heterogeneous formats to one consistent representation so the model gets clean data every time.

options.label: B
options.body: A PreToolUse hook that rewrites the outgoing tool calls before they are sent out to each of the MCP servers.
options.rationale: PreToolUse acts on outgoing calls, not on returned results — it can't normalize tool output.

options.label: C
options.body: Instructions in the system prompt telling the model how to parse each of the different timestamp and status formats it encounters.
options.rationale: Probabilistic and brittle across many formats; a deterministic normalization hook is more reliable.

options.label: D
options.body: Ask each MCP server owner to standardize the timestamp and status formats their own tools return to a common representation.
options.rationale: Often out of your control and slow; a PostToolUse hook fixes it in one place on your side.

stem: A coordinator needs three independent subagents (web search, patent lookup, news scan) whose work doesn't depend on each other. How should it spawn them to minimize latency?

options.label: A
options.body: Emit multiple Task tool calls in a single coordinator response to spawn them in parallel.
options.rationale: Correct. Independent subagents should be spawned with parallel Task calls in one turn — sequential spawning across separate turns adds unnecessary latency.

options.label: B
options.body: Spawn them one per turn, feeding each one's output into the next.
options.rationale: They're independent, so chaining them serially wastes time for no benefit.

options.label: C
options.body: Have the first subagent spawn the other two subagents itself once it has started running its own work.
options.rationale: Subagents don't spawn siblings; nested spawning hides execution from the coordinator and hurts observability.

options.label: D
options.body: Use fork_session to run the three subagents as three separate branches of the same underlying session.
options.rationale: Forking is for exploring divergent approaches from a shared baseline, not for fanning out independent parallel tasks.
